# LLM-based Vulnerability Detection at Project Scale: An Empirical Study

- Authors: Li, Fengjie; Jiang, Jiajun; Chen, Dongchi; Xiong, Yingfei
- Year / venue: 2026, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1109/tse.2026.3742453 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/tse.2026.3742453
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Our PDF is arXiv:2601.19239v2 (25 Sep 2026, stamp on p. 1), not the IEEE version of record; page numbers and possibly some numbers may differ from the TSE copy.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Systematically evaluate specialized project-scale LLM-based vulnerability detectors against general-purpose coding agents and traditional static analyzers on (a) known vulnerabilities and (b) current real-world projects, explaining their false positives and measuring their cost [A] (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: How effective are LLM-based methods at detecting known vulnerabilities in a controlled benchmark? [V] (p. 3)
- RQ2: How reliable are they on real-world projects/modules, in terms of false discovery rates? [V] (p. 3)
- RQ3: What are the root causes of false positives? [V] (p. 4)
- RQ4: What is the overhead (tokens, money, time) of project-scale LLM detection? [V] (p. 4)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: comparative empirical benchmark study, plus qualitative FP root-cause taxonomy (open coding, double coding) and LLM-assisted (Codex) labelling with stratified manual validation [V] (p. 6, p. 11, p. 13).
- Approach / model / intervention (Table I, p. 4) [V]:
  - Specialized LLM-based: RepoAudit (multi-agent; Claude Sonnet 3.5 / GPT-5.4; C/C++; CWE-401/416/476), KNighter (LLM-synthesised Clang Static Analyzer checkers; o3-mini / GPT-5.4; C/C++), IRIS (LLM-inferred sources/sinks + CodeQL; GPT-4 / GPT-5.4; Java; CWE-022/078/079/094), LLMDFA (multi-agent dataflow; GPT-4 / GPT-5.4; Java; CWE-078/079), INFERROI (LLM intent inference + CFG; GPT-4 / GPT-5.4; Java; CWE-772) (p. 4, p. 5).
  - General agents: Codex (GPT-5.4) and Claude Code (Claude Sonnet 4.6), all CWEs, internet search disabled (p. 4, p. 7).
  - Each specialized method run with its original backbone and with GPT-5.4 to separate model from workflow effects (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: traditional SAST — CodeQL (48 selected rules, C/C++ and Java), Semgrep (59 rules, C/C++ and Java), SpotBugs + Find Security Bugs (21 patterns, Java), Clang Static Analyzer CSA (12 checkers, C/C++) [V] (p. 4, p. 7). Rules were manually curated to the target CWEs; all severities treated equally [V] (p. 7). No deep-learning (fine-tuned/GNN) detectors and no prompt-only/RAG function-level methods (excluded because they do not produce repository-level warnings) [V] (p. 4). LLMxCPG excluded (needs local fine-tuning) [V] (p. 4).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): controlled dataset from ReposVul (C/C++), CWE-Bench-Java (Maven projects only) and JLeaks (50 randomly sampled resource leaks); all cases manually checked for validity and successful compilation [V] (p. 5). Real-world dataset: 24 actively maintained projects/modules with historical vulnerabilities in the studied CWEs (e.g. Linux subsystems, ImageMagick, Vim, gpac, bitlbee; OpenOLAT, Spark, DSpace, XStream, Jenkins, Keycloak, Tika, xwiki, ActiveMQ, RxJava, jsoup) [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 265 known vulnerabilities — C/C++: CWE-401 50, CWE-416 25, CWE-476 35; Java: CWE-022 49, CWE-078 11, CWE-079 28, CWE-094 17, CWE-772 50 [V] (p. 6). 24 projects/modules sized 1,715 to 6,033,855 LOC [V] (p. 6). Up to 300 warnings sampled per tool per project → 6,442 warnings; 5,896 FPs classified; 355 warnings manually coded to build the taxonomy (>150 person-hours) [V] (p. 6, p. 11, p. 13).
- Sampling / selection method: for ReposVul, the three repositories with most cases per CWE (to limit build effort); 8 CWEs chosen by tool support and benchmark availability [V] (p. 5). 21 of 24 real-world commits postdate the August 2025 knowledge cutoff of GPT-5.4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 [V] (p. 5). Several C/C++ modules come from the same Linux commit [A] (p. 18). No power analysis.
- Data availability (public? link?): artifacts (scripts, prompts, taxonomy labels, statistics) at https://github.com/Feng-Jay/LLM4Security [V] (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: released replication packages of each specialized tool with hyper-parameters from the original papers; no extra timeouts or token/money budgets [V] (p. 6). Default RepoAudit configuration; IRIS/LLMDFA/INFERROI use their own LLM-generated API lists; KNighter checkers generated from 18 bug-fixing patches from its original study [V] (p. 7). General agents via official CLIs with built-in tools/skills, internet off [V] (p. 7). Official OpenAI/Anthropic APIs; local server with dual Xeon 6388, 512 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04.6 [V] (p. 7). Each LLM configuration run once [A] (p. 18).
- Controlled-dataset TP rule: a vulnerability counts as detected if the tool reports the labelled vulnerable program point; FPs are warnings in known vulnerable files that do not match the known data-flow pattern (IRIS protocol) [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
- Real-world labelling: Codex labels each sampled warning TP/FP with access to the repository; validation on up to 5 TPs + 5 FPs per tool per repo (197 TPs, 424 FPs) [V] (p. 11).
- Code availability: yes, project homepage above [V] (p. 2). Appendices A–C (FP examples, rule lists, detailed cost statistics) are referenced but are not in our 20-page PDF (p. 7, p. 13, p. 15).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - Recall = TP/(TP+FN) and Precision = TP/(TP+FP) on the controlled set, following prior studies [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
  - #Reports, #Files, #Sampled FPs and SFDR = #Sampled FPs / #Sampled Reports on real-world projects, because ground truth is unknown there [V] (p. 6).
  - Input/output tokens, USD and end-to-end minutes per project/module; cost and minutes per warning [V] (p. 6, p. 15, p. 16).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): no significance tests between tools. Labelling accuracy estimated with stratified sampling, normal approximation and finite-population correction at the 95% level [V] (p. 11, p. 13); the intervals themselves are not printed in the text we have.

## 7. Key findings
1. C/C++ controlled set: general agents average recall 59.55% (131/220) and precision 32.19% (131/407); KNighter detects 0 vulnerabilities in all three CWEs; RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) detects 2 (CWE-476 recall 5.71%) — [V] (p. 7, Table IV).
2. C/C++ per CWE (Table IV): CWE-401 Codex R 68.00% / P 41.98%, Claude Code R 80.00% / P 40.00%, CodeQL R 6.00% / P 14.29%, Semgrep and CSA 0%; CWE-416 Codex R 40.00%, Claude Code R 36.00%, CodeQL/Semgrep/CSA 0%; CWE-476 Codex R 62.86%, Claude Code R 45.71%, CodeQL R 34.29% with 1,110 warnings (P 1.08%) — [V] (p. 7).
3. Java controlled set: Codex average recall 63.87% (99/155), Claude Code 81.94% (127/155); CodeQL 14.19%, Semgrep 6.67%, SpotBugs 14.84%; LLMDFA (GPT-5.4) finds 1 vulnerability; INFERROI (GPT-5.4) reaches 66.00% recall on CWE-772 vs CodeQL 10.00% and SpotBugs 6.00% — [V] (p. 9, Table VI p. 10).
4. Java precision is low for most tools (e.g. CWE-022: IRIS GPT-4 6.30%, Semgrep 0.29% from 2,075 warnings, SpotBugs 1.76%, Codex 58.73%, Claude Code 37.29%) — [V] (p. 10, Table VI).
5. Swapping in GPT-5.4 barely changes recall of specialized methods but raises some precision (IRIS CWE-078 6.06% → 20.00%; INFERROI 15.74% → 20.50%); authors conclude workflow, not model, limits recall — [V]/[A] (p. 9).
6. Incomplete API modelling and incomplete candidate exploration explain 108/108 (RepoAudit GPT-5.4), 97/110 (KNighter GPT-5.4), 40/44 (Codex) and 40/45 (Claude Code) missed C/C++ vulnerabilities — [V] (p. 7). With perfect allocation/deallocation API specs on CWE-401, recall rises: RepoAudit 0 → 48%, Codex 68 → 90%, Claude Code 80 → 96%, CodeQL 6 → 56% — [V] (p. 8, Table V).
7. Missed vulnerabilities for general agents sit in larger files (Fig. 4/6); IRIS and INFERROI are largely unaffected because they reason over compact representations — [V]/[A] (p. 9, p. 10).
8. LLM-based tools contribute most unique detections; traditional tools add few unique ones (CodeQL at most 3 unique on CWE-022) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10, Fig. 5).
9. Real-world C/C++ (Table VII): overall SFDR RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) 92.77%, KNighter (o3-mini) 81.25%, Codex 9.09% (2.44 warnings/project), Claude Code 74.07%, CodeQL 86.01% (752.67 warnings/project; 6,345 on gpac), Semgrep 100.00%, CSA 85.51% — [V] (p. 11). GPT-5.4 versions: RepoAudit 95.41%, KNighter 95.56% (Table VIII) — [V] (p. 11).
10. Real-world Java (Table IX): IRIS (GPT-4) 97.80% SFDR with 232.42 warnings/project, LLMDFA 100.00%, INFERROI 96.40%, Codex 31.82% (1.47 warnings/project), Claude Code 81.82%, CodeQL 77.00%, Semgrep 92.71%, SpotBugs 86.21%; traditional tools emit warnings in only about half of projects — [V] (p. 12). IRIS with GPT-5.4 drops to 78.73% (Table X) — [V] (p. 12).
11. Codex labels were 94.36% accurate on 621 manually validated warnings (population-weighted 98.16%); Codex FP-reason labels 87.76% accurate on 425 cases (weighted 92.52%) — [V] (p. 11, p. 13).
12. FP root causes: incorrect program-point classification B1 = 63.33% (3,734/5,896) and truncated interprocedural context A1 = 14.60% (861/5,896); LLM tools additionally show incorrect control flow (A2), missed sanitizers/guards (D1, >15% in 7 of 12 LLM settings) and prompt deviations (C1) — [V] (p. 15, Table XI p. 14). CodeQL's largest FP causes are A1 35.80% and path-insensitivity D3 20.17% — [V] (p. 14).
13. Cost (Table XII): RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) up to 225,493.97K input and 38,078.26K output tokens and $1,247.66 for one project, average $172.77; LLMDFA (GPT-4) average $61.60 and 2,000 min per Java project (max 4,638 min); IRIS (GPT-4) average $2.59, 213.44 min; INFERROI average $11.62–$12.99; KNighter $0.34–$2.36; Codex $5.38 / 14.80 min; Claude Code $9.67 / 13.19 min per project. SAST average runtimes 0.64 (Semgrep) to 60.92 (CSA) minutes, no token cost — [V] (p. 16).
14. Per warning: Codex $2.93 and 8.1 min, Claude Code $1.77 and 2.4 min; LLMDFA >$24 and >800 min per warning — [V] (p. 15, p. 16).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Controlled evaluation counts warnings about other, unlabelled genuine vulnerabilities as FPs (p. 18).
- [A] Each LLM configuration run once; nondeterminism may affect results (p. 18).
- [A] Taxonomy and labels involve expert judgement; large-scale labels partly come from Codex and may contain model bias (p. 18).
- [A] Pretraining contamination possible for both datasets; post-cutoff commits may retain older code; sessions showed no explicit reliance on CVE data (p. 18).
- [A] Tool selection, two languages (C/C++, Java), 8 CWEs; several Linux modules share one repository/commit; no concurrency or type-confusion bugs; may not generalise to Rust, Go, TypeScript or multi-language projects (p. 18).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Codex (GPT-5.4) is both an evaluated detector and the main TP/FP labeller and FP-reason classifier. Codex has by far the lowest SFDR (9.09% C/C++, 31.82% Java). Validation was stratified (≤5 TPs + ≤5 FPs per tool per repo), so a judge that favours its own reports is only partly ruled out; per-tool labelling accuracy is not reported. Based on p. 11 and Tables VII/IX.
- [I] The low SFDRs of general agents rest on very few warnings (Codex: 2.44 × 9 ≈ 22 C/C++ and 1.47 × 15 ≈ 22 Java warnings), so they are imprecise; no per-tool confidence intervals are shown. Based on Tables VII and IX (p. 11, p. 12).
- [I] Controlled-set precision only counts FPs inside known vulnerable files, so it is not project-wide precision and is not comparable with SFDR or with precision in other papers. Based on p. 6.
- [I] SAST rule sets were curated by the authors (48/59/21/12 rules); other rule choices could change SAST recall and FP counts. Based on p. 7.
- [I] The controlled benchmark uses public CVEs that likely predate model training; general agents' high controlled recall may partly reflect memorisation even without explicit lookup. The post-cutoff real-world set gives no recall, so recall on unseen code is not measured. Based on p. 5, p. 18.
- [I] No deep-learning (fine-tuned) detectors are compared: informs LLM vs SAST, not LLM vs DL. Based on p. 4.
- [I] Backbones differ across tools (Claude Sonnet 4.6 vs GPT-5.4 vs GPT-4), so agent-vs-specialized comparisons mix workflow and model effects, partly controlled by the GPT-5.4 re-runs. Based on Table I (p. 4).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): LLM self-labelling (see 9); pretraining contamination acknowledged (p. 18); single runs (p. 18); different backbones per tool (p. 4).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ and Java only, 8 CWEs, 24 projects with several from one Linux commit (p. 18); tools limited to publicly available, runnable ones (p. 4).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): SFDR measures false alarms among sampled warnings, not missed vulnerabilities; controlled precision is file-restricted (p. 6); all SAST severities counted equally (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no significance tests between tools; small warning counts for some tools; no run-to-run variance.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — artifacts, prompts and rule lists released (p. 2, p. 7); API model versions may change.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: combine flexible agents with program-analysis support such as path constraints, IRs and validators (p. 17); integrate LLMs with formal analysis/symbolic execution (p. 17); evidence-grounded API-role/specification inference with iterative validation (p. 17); explicit modelling of ownership, sanitizers, error paths and resource lifecycles (p. 17); structured multi-agent or self-verification for prompt compliance (p. 17); cost-aware designs — hierarchical/incremental analysis, caching, adaptive LLM invocation, cheaper models (p. 18); broader languages and CWE classes (p. 18).
- Suggested by us [I]: an independent (non-evaluated) judge or full manual labelling for warning triage; repeated runs with variance; LLM vs DL vs SAST on the same post-cutoff projects with recall measured via newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few head-to-head project-scale comparisons of LLM detectors and SAST (CodeQL, Semgrep, SpotBugs, CSA) on the same targets, with recall, precision/SFDR and cost. It shows "LLM vs SAST" depends heavily on the LLM workflow: general agents beat SAST on recall, specialized hybrids (IRIS, INFERROI, KNighter) often do not. Gives concrete cost data for RQ3 and an FP taxonomy shared by both families for RQ5.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|

# RepoAudit: An Autonomous LLM-Agent for Repository-Level Code Auditing

- Authors: Guo, Jinyao; Wang, Chengpeng; Xu, Xiangzhe; Su, Zian; Zhang, Xiangyu
- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2501.18160 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18160
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Our PDF is arXiv:2501.18160v3 (29 May 2025). Its p. 1 already carries the footer "Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025" (p. 1), so it appears to be the camera-ready text, but rlab records the paper as an arXiv preprint.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Build and evaluate an LLM agent that audits whole C/C++ repositories for path-sensitive memory bugs without compilation, overcoming context limits, hallucination and cost of direct prompting [A] (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No explicit RQs. Implicit questions: effectiveness on known bugs, comparison with LLM-based and industrial detectors, contribution of components (ablation), sensitivity to model and temperature, real-world impact [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
- Underlying claim: LLMs are good at function-local abstraction, pointer handling and feasible-path exploration, but poor at whole-repository reasoning [A] (p. 3, p. 4).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: design-and-evaluate tool paper with comparative experiments, ablations and a field deployment [V] (p. 7, p. 8, p. 15).
- Approach / model / intervention: three components [V] (p. 5–7): an initiator (tree-sitter pattern matchers find source values, e.g. NULL literals); an explorer that prompts the LLM one function at a time to derive data-flow facts along feasible paths, stores them in agent memory (also used as a cache) and moves to callers/callees on demand; a validator that checks control-flow order of data-flow facts with a parser and asks the LLM whether inter-procedural path conditions are satisfiable. Calling-context bound K = 4 functions, temperature 0.0, default model Claude 3.5 Sonnet [V] (p. 7).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: Meta Infer and Amazon CodeGuru (industrial static analyzers) [V] (p. 8, p. 14); single-function and multiple-function few-shot CoT prompting and the LLMDFA agent (only on functions related to RepoAudit's TPs, or reachable from sources) [V] (p. 13). No open-source SAST such as CodeQL/Semgrep/CSA, no deep-learning detectors.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): 15 projects (5 per bug type) taken from bug reports of prior papers (Huang et al. 2024; Shi et al. 2021, 2018) [V] (p. 7). NPD: sofa-pbrpc, ImageMagick/MagickCore, coturn, libfreenect, openldap; MLK: libsass, memcached, linux/driver/net, linux/sound, linux/mm; UAF: Redis, linux/drivers/peci, shadowsocks-libev, wabt-tool, icu i18n; 2,130–1,378,262 LoC [V] (p. 7, Table 1).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 15 projects with 21 previously reported bugs (counted as "Old" TPs) [V] (p. 8, p. 17); 9 further projects of 14K–1.7M LoC (avg 420K LoC) for the field study [V] (p. 8).
- Sampling / selection method: "well-maintained" projects from prior bug reports [A] (p. 7). The paper says both "ten actively maintained repositories" (p. 2) and "nine open-source GitHub projects" (p. 8, p. 9); Table 4 lists nine [V] (p. 9).
- Data availability (public? link?): code at https://github.com/PurCL/RepoAudit [V] (p. 1). A labelled dataset release is not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: tree-sitter for parsing/call graphs; Claude 3.5 Sonnet at temperature 0; K = 4 [V] (p. 7). Additional runs with DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and OpenAI o3-mini, and temperatures 0.25–1.0 [V] (p. 16, p. 17). Infer tried in v1.2.0, v1.0.0 and v0.9.0; 2 projects failed to build and 5 crashed or were incompatible [V] (p. 15). Infer and CodeGuru reports were manually labelled TP/FP [V] (p. 14). How RepoAudit's own reports were judged TP or FP (who labelled, criteria, agreement) is not reported.
- Code availability: yes (p. 1).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: TP, FP, precision = TP/(TP+FP); "recall" is the share of the 21 previously reported bugs reproduced (p. 17); prompting rounds, input/output tokens, USD and seconds per project (p. 8). Overall recall against all bugs in the projects is not measured.
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none; single run per setting (temperature study gives one run per temperature) [V] (p. 17).

## 7. Key findings
1. RepoAudit (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) reproduces all 21 known bugs and finds 19 new ones (14 fixed in the latest commit): 40 TPs, 11 FPs, precision 78.43%; 21 TPs are inter-procedural — [V] (p. 7, Table 2 p. 8).
2. Cost: average 0.44 h (1,577.22 s), 100.67 prompts, 614,625.73 input and 46,153.07 output tokens, $2.54 per project, $0.95 per true bug; most expensive project (icu) $18.15 and 10,661.98 s — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
3. Meta Infer: 13 projects build but 5 crash; on 8 analysed projects 7 TPs and 2 FPs, no MLK or UAF bug found — [V] (p. 8, p. 15). Amazon CodeGuru (NPD and UAF only, 10 projects): 0 TPs and 18 FPs — [V] (p. 8, p. 15).
4. LLM baselines: single-function CoT finds 1 true bug, multiple-function CoT 10; LLMDFA needs on average 165.23× (path scan) to 1,737.04× (source scan) the prompts and 123.18×–1,193.63× the input tokens of RepoAudit — [V] (p. 8, p. 14).
5. Ablations: without abstraction TPs −47.50%, FPs +181.82% (precision 40.38%); without validators FPs +245.45% (31 FPs); without caching ~3.5× prompts, 3.48× cost, 3.75× time, icu exceeds 72 h — [V] (p. 8, p. 15, p. 16).
6. Other models: DeepSeek R1 46 TPs, precision 88.46%, $0.57 but 4,571.72 s per project; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 46 TPs, 86.79%, $1.59; o3-mini 42 TPs, 82.35%, $0.30, ~625 s — [V] (p. 8, p. 16, p. 17).
7. Temperature 0–1.0: precision 72.92–78.43%, recall of known bugs 85.71–100% — [V] (p. 17, Table 11).
8. Field study on 9 projects: 185 new bugs reported at 85.71% precision; 95 confirmed and 79 fixed (174 total); libuv (86 NPD) and memcached (67 MLK) dominate — [V] (p. 8, p. 9, Table 4).
9. 19 of 25 CWE Top-25 (2024) weaknesses need global path-sensitive reasoning — [A] (p. 3).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] FPs and FNs from LLM hallucination (p. 9).
- [A] Cost is highly sensitive to the number of source elements in a repository (p. 9).
- [A] Not sound inter-procedurally: limited to four functions, may miss bugs with longer call chains (p. 9).
- [A] FP example: unaware of external (YANG schema) constraints; FN example: Claude 3.5 Sonnet missed an error-handling path (p. 18).
- [A] Possible leakage of private source code to LLM providers and token costs (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Evaluation by the tool's own authors; the TP/FP judgement procedure for RepoAudit's reports is not described, while Infer/CodeGuru reports were "manually" checked (p. 14). Based on p. 7–8, p. 14.
- [I] Recall is only measured on 21 previously reported bugs (one per project for most), so true recall is unknown; FNs beyond these are not counted. Based on Table 2 (p. 8) and Table 11 (p. 17).
- [I] Industrial baselines are disadvantaged by build failures and crashes (Infer analysed only 8/15 projects); no compile-free open-source SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL build-less modes) or CSA baseline. Based on p. 15.
- [I] Benchmark projects come from prior papers' public bug reports, so model memorisation of known bugs cannot be excluded; not discussed. Based on p. 7.
- [I] Internal inconsistencies: "ten" (p. 2) vs "nine" (p. 8, p. 9) field-study repositories; Table 4 MLK TP column sums to 75 while the printed total is 76 (NPD 107 + MLK 75 + UAF 3 = 185, matching the text; the 85.71% precision matches 186/217). Based on Table 4 (p. 9).
- [I] Contradicts later independent evaluation: li2026llm re-ran RepoAudit on overlapping targets (linux/mm, linux/sound, linux/drivers/net, linux/drivers/peci, ImageMagick) and found 0 detections on known CWE-401/416 cases and 92.77% SFDR. Based on li2026llm Tables IV and VII.
- [I] "Bugs" (NPD/MLK/UAF) are memory-safety defects, not necessarily exploitable vulnerabilities.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): author-evaluated; labelling procedure not reported; possible pretraining exposure to known bugs; baselines restricted to RepoAudit-related functions in the LLM comparison (p. 13).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ only, 3 bug types, 15 + 9 projects (p. 7, p. 9).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): "recall" = reproduction of 21 known bugs, not overall recall (p. 17).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests; one run per configuration; small counts (11 FPs).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code public (p. 1); prompts partly shown (p. 6, p. 7); full labelled report set not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: stronger or fine-tuned models for sub-tasks such as feasible-path exploration (p. 9); a richer compilation-free tool suite to expose branches/loops to the model (p. 9); extension to other languages (Python, JavaScript) (p. 10).
- Suggested by us [I]: independent replication with blinded labelling and recall on unseen, post-cutoff bugs; comparison with build-free SAST (Semgrep) and CSA on identical targets.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: a representative agentic LLM detector with explicit cost data and a direct comparison with industrial static analyzers (Infer, CodeGuru). Its strong self-reported precision vs li2026llm's independent replication is a key contradiction for RQ1/RQ2 and illustrates how evaluation setup drives reported results.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |

## 14. Key quotes
> "In total, it reports 40 TPs and 11 FPs, resulting in a precision of 78.43%." (p. 7)

> "Amazon CODEGURU reports 18 false positives (FPs) with no true positives (TPs), while Meta INFER also only reports seven TPs along with two FPs." (p. 2)

> "it currently limits flow analysis to a maximum of four functions" (p. 9)

The ICML 2025 (PMLR 267) proceedings version exists per the footer on p. 1 and li2026llm's reference list; we did not compare with the PMLR copy, so published numbers may differ slightly. Metadata still records it as an arXiv preprint (tier 3); consider re-adding via the published record if rlab can resolve it.
- Uncertainties: the CodeGuru quote has the small-caps name split by extraction ("C ODE G URU"); the wording is otherwise verbatim. The confirmed (95) and fixed (79) counts are treated by the authors as disjoint (sum 174) (p. 2, p. 9).

# Benchmarking LLMs and LLM-based Agents in Practical Vulnerability Detection for Code Repositories

- Authors: Yildiz, Alperen; Teo, Sin G; Lou, Yiling; Feng, Yebo; Wang, Chong; Divakaran, Dinil Mon
- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) (published)
- DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.1490 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.1490
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index; printed pages 30848–30865). Identity confirmed: title and authors on p. 1 match metadata.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Provide a practical benchmark for just-in-time (JIT, i.e. commit-triggered) repository-level vulnerability detection with interprocedural context and pairwise (vulnerable vs patched) evaluation, and use it to compare LLMs with LLM-based ReAct agents [A] (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No numbered RQs. Four comparisons: detection method (p. 7), prompting strategy (p. 8), foundation model (p. 8), pairwise error analysis (p. 8) [V].
- Three stated requirements for practical benchmarks: interprocedural context, scalability, pairwise comparison [V] (p. 3, p. 4).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: benchmark construction plus comparative evaluation [V] (p. 4, p. 5).
- Approach / model / intervention: (1) Plain LLM — target function only; (2) Dep-Aug LLM — adds Top-5 lexically similar callers/callees (Jaccard), reproducing VulEval; (3) ReAct agent with tools get_callers, get_callees, get_definition (CFlow + CTags, LangChain) [V] (p. 5, p. 6). Each in four variants: vanilla, CoT ("Solve this problem step by step..."), few-shot (10 hand-made vulnerable/benign pairs from CWE Top-25 web pages), CoT+FS [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: the three LLM settings against each other; no SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors [V] (p. 5). A random-guessing reference (22.70%) is cited from Ding et al. (p. 7).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): PrimeVul (CVE fixed in a single commit modifying a single function); vul-intro commit approximated by tracing the target function's history back to its last modification into the vulnerable version [V] (p. 4, p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 879 CVEs, 91 CWEs (max 10 CVEs per CWE), 1,758 samples (879 vul, 879 ben) [V] (p. 4, p. 5). Repositories: mean 2,955.9 files, 91% C / 9% C++, mean 988.8 KLoC (median 297.6, SD 1,991.2); target function mean 696.4 LOC [V] (p. 5).
- Sampling / selection method: random selection of 879 PrimeVul CVEs ensuring CWE coverage [V] (p. 4).
- Data availability (public? link?): "We release all code and data at this repository" (p. 2); the URL is a hyperlink not present in the extracted text.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o at temperature 0; Transformers v4.52.0, LangChain v0.3.14 [V] (p. 6). Llama-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-16B in Appendix B [V] (p. 8, p. 15). Number of runs: not reported (one implied by temperature 0). Number of pairs evaluated per setting: not reported (see Analyst notes). Token use, cost and runtime: not reported.
- Code availability: yes, per p. 2.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: F1 (common metric) and pairwise accuracy pAcc = share of pairs where both versions are labelled correctly, inspired by PrimeVul, to test whether methods capture the vulnerability rather than surface patterns [V] (p. 6). Error types: pairwise vulnerable, pairwise benign, pairwise reversed [V] (p. 8).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. GPT-4o-mini F1/pAcc — Plain: 56.00/3.36 (vanilla), 65.10/3.36 (CoT), 48.74/7.56 (FS), 64.65/11.76 (CoT+FS); Dep-Aug: 52.68/2.05, 66.05/4.86, 48.23/7.27, 65.01/4.68; ReAct: 56.63/12.61, 56.93/16.81, 56.81/20.17, 51.06/14.29 — [V] (p. 6, Table 2).
2. GPT-4o F1/pAcc — Plain: 65.96/1.02, 62.22/15.02, 62.77/4.44, 64.44/17.63; Dep-Aug: 63.30/1.03, 62.60/18.66, 62.03/2.39, 61.12/18.79; ReAct: 57.77/17.63, 58.07/19.13, 56.42/18.91, 52.61/18.89 — [V] (p. 6, Table 2).
3. ReAct agents have higher pAcc than other methods for every prompting strategy (gains 0.1 to 16.61 points); Plain/Dep-Aug have higher F1 in most settings (4.15–13.95 points) — [V] (p. 7). Average ReAct pAcc gain over Dep-Aug: 9.46 (4o-mini) and 8.42 (4o) — [V] (p. 7).
4. LLM methods label >90% of samples vulnerable in some settings; precision is around 50% for all methods on the balanced benchmark, so F1 rewards over-prediction — [V]/[A] (p. 7).
5. On the original non-paired PrimeVul test set (695 vul / 25,216 ben), GPT-4o-mini F1 falls to 5.41–12.21 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
6. Dep-Aug does not consistently beat Plain and sometimes lowers pAcc, possibly due to noisy retrieved context — [V]/[A] (p. 7).
7. The most common pairwise error is "both vulnerable": ~40–95% for LLMs, ~35–50% for ReAct — [V] (p. 8).
8. ReAct calls tools far more on the vulnerable than the benign version (5.85 vs 1.79, GPT-4o-mini vanilla) — inconsistent analysis — [V] (p. 9).
9. Llama-3.1-8B ReAct agents often fail output formatting and default to "benign" (F1 3.28–14.67); DeepSeek-Coder-V2 Dep-Aug with CoT+FS reaches F1 82.09 and pAcc 69.24, the best result in the paper, while its ReAct agent stays at pAcc ≤21.39 — [V] (p. 8, p. 15, Table 4).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Vul-intro commits may be traced imperfectly; some instances manually inspected (p. 9).
- [A] Label-balanced dataset may bias F1 comparisons (p. 9).
- [A] Missing statistics such as the share of interprocedural vulnerabilities; annotation hard to scale (p. 9).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] No SAST or deep-learning baselines and no cost data, so the paper cannot answer LLM-vs-SAST/DL questions directly. Based on p. 5–6.
- [I] All GPT-4o/4o-mini settings have pAcc ≤20.17%, below the 25% expected from independent random labelling of each pair member; "ReAct is better" means "less bad". Based on Table 2 (p. 6).
- [I] The headline "ReAct agents better at pairwise" is not robust across models: with DeepSeek-Coder-V2, Dep-Aug LLM is far better (pAcc 69.24 vs ≤21.39). Based on Table 4 (p. 15).
- [I] Data leakage is not discussed: PrimeVul CVEs and fixes are public and likely in GPT-4o training data. Based on p. 4 (no contamination analysis found in the text).
- [I] No repeated runs, variance or significance tests; differences of a few points (e.g. 0.1-point pAcc gain) are not interpretable. Based on p. 6–7.
- [I] Few-shot examples are single-function CWE web-page snippets, which may not suit interprocedural agents (authors note this too, p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): possible pretraining contamination; vul-intro approximation (p. 9); unclear per-setting sample sizes.
- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ only (91% C), PrimeVul single-function fixes, OpenAI models mainly (p. 5, p. 6).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): pAcc captures discrimination of vulnerable vs patched code; F1 on a balanced set overstates usefulness (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, no variance, many configurations compared.
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code and data released (p. 2); prompts in Appendix A (p. 12, p. 13).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking; agent-oriented prompting strategies; robust reasoning models for vulnerability analysis (p. 2, p. 8); more benign commits for F1 (p. 9); code-specific LLMs optimised for agents (p. 15); integrate constraint solving or program analysis (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]: add SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep) and fine-tuned DL baselines on JITVul pairs; report cost and contamination checks.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only), RQ2, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: mainly methodological evidence for RQ2 — F1 on balanced data looks moderate (~50–66%) while pairwise accuracy shows near-random discrimination, explaining why reported LLM effectiveness varies across studies. No direct LLM-vs-SAST comparison.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | GPT-4o/4o-mini plain, dependency-augmented and ReAct detectors reach F1 48–66% but pairwise accuracy only 1.02–20.17% on 879 CVE pairs | p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | ReAct agents give the highest pAcc for every prompting strategy with GPT-4o/4o-mini (gains up to 16.61 points) | p. 7 | V | weak |
| RQ2 | F1 is distribution-sensitive: GPT-4o-mini F1 drops from ~49–65% (balanced pairs) to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul (695 vul / 25,216 ben) | p. 6, p. 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | LLM methods label >90% of samples vulnerable in some settings, with precision ~50%, inflating F1 | p. 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | With DeepSeek-Coder-V2, Dep-Aug LLM reaches F1 82.09 / pAcc 69.24, contradicting the agent advantage seen with GPT models | p. 15 | V | weak |
| RQ5 | Most frequent failure is labelling both vulnerable and patched versions vulnerable (40–95% of LLM failures); agents analyse pairs inconsistently | p. 8, p. 9 | V | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "A higher F1 score does not necessarily indicate a detection method's superior ability to capture vulnerability characteristics." (p. 7)

> "precision remains similar across methods, around 50%, as observed on our label-balanced benchmark" (p. 7)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 18 PDF pages read, including Appendices A–C (prompts, Llama/DeepSeek results, case studies CVE-2019-15164 and CVE-2019-3877).
- Uncertainties: the number of pairs per setting is not stated. Every Plain and ReAct pAcc for GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1 is an exact multiple of 1/119 (e.g. 3.36 = 4/119, 20.17 = 24/119, 0.84 = 1/119), while GPT-4o values match k/879. This suggests some settings were evaluated on ~119 pairs, or after excluding failed runs, but the paper does not say so; treat cross-setting comparisons cautiously ([I], arithmetic on Table 2 p. 6 and Table 4 p. 15). "Improvements ... 0.1% to 16.61%" are percentage points. The 22.70% random-guessing figure is cited from Ding et al., not computed here (p. 7). Quote 2 is joined across a hyphenated line break ("sim-ilar").

# To Think or Not to Think: Evaluating LLM Reasoning and Agents in Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Tan, Hua Beng; Widyasari, Ratnadira; Astekin, Merve; Goknil, Arda; Sözer, Hasan; Tun, Yan Naing; Husom, Erik Johannes; Shar, Lwin Khin; Jiang, Lingxiao
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837521 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837521
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` from the user-supplied publisher PDF (ACM version of record, ASE '26, 13 pages, printed pp. 2856–2868; page refs = PDF page index).

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Separate the effects of reasoning-enabled ("thinking") inference, agentic orchestration and explanation quality on LLM vulnerability detection, which prior work examined separately or under heterogeneous settings [A] (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: Do reasoning-enabled LLMs outperform non-reasoning LLMs in software vulnerability detection? [V] (p. 2)
- RQ2: How do multi-agent configurations compare with single-agent setups in performance, cross-setting stability and improvement consistency? [V] (p. 2)
- RQ3: How does explanation quality differ between thinking and non-thinking LLMs? [V] (p. 2)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled, factor-separated (factorial) experiment. RQ1: 4 models × 2 modes × 2 prompting strategies, non-agent = 16 configurations; RQ2: same × 3 agent designs = 48 configurations; RQ3 on the generated outputs [V] (p. 3, Table 1). Additional call-matched and role-sensitivity experiments (p. 10, p. 11).
- Approach / model / intervention: Nemotron-Nano-8B, Nemotron-Super-49B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, each in instruct and thinking mode [V] (p. 3, p. 4). Designs: NA (direct call, no state); SA (one agent); DA (Code Author proposes, Security Analyst reviews and decides); MA (Security Researcher, Code Author, Moderator, Review Board) [V] (p. 4). Zero-shot and few-shot prompts with identical structure and examples across models/modes [V] (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: instruct mode vs thinking mode; SA as the agentic baseline; call-matched self-revision with 2 and 4 calls, best-of-4 at T = 0.7, and VulAgent-lite (a specialist hypothesis–validation workflow without Joern CFG/DFG) [V] (p. 10, p. 11). No SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors, no proprietary LLMs as detectors.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): PrimeVul Pair; each vulnerable function paired with a benign counterpart sharing ≥80% of its string content; the counterpart is not shown at inference [V] (p. 3, p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 870 functions (435 vulnerable, 435 benign) per configuration [V] (p. 3); call-matched experiments on a pair-preserving 193-pair subset, 2 largest models, zero-shot [V] (p. 11). RQ3: 120 explanations (60 snippets × 2 modes, 15 per TP/TN/FP/FN) rated by 2 blinded humans; paired tests on 59 pairs; LLM judge on a 480-explanation frame (2 models × 2 modes × 4 strata × 30) [V] (p. 5, p. 9).
- Sampling / selection method: full PrimeVul Pair set for RQ1/RQ2; how the 193-pair subset was chosen is not reported beyond "pair-preserving" (p. 11). No power analysis.
- Data availability (public? link?): replication package with code, prompts and dataset on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21401826 [V] (p. 5, p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: vLLM v0.17–v0.18, 64K context window, NVIDIA H100 80GB on RunPod; temperature 0; pilot repetitions showed no variation, so one run per configuration [V] (p. 4). Agents built with the AG2 framework [V] (p. 4). Outputs auto-parsed to binary labels; non-conforming outputs "handled conservatively" (exact rule not reported) [V] (p. 5). LLM judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 24 few-shot exemplars from held-out human ratings, validated by 5-fold cross-validation against the inter-human agreement level; Claude Opus 4.8 tried as an alternative [V] (p. 5, p. 9). Cost assumes RunPod H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hour [V] (p. 10).
- Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (directly interpretable because the data are balanced); P-C, the share of pairs where both functions are classified correctly, to measure discrimination between near-identical code (following Ding et al.) [V] (p. 5). Alert burden: false-positive rate and predicted-positive rate [V] (p. 7). Stability: mean F1, SD and coefficient of variation across settings; improvement consistency = share of matched settings beating SA [V] (p. 5). Explanations: completeness, informativeness, clarity, actionability on 1–5 Likert scales [V] (p. 5). Cost: GPU-hours, kWh, input/output tokens, USD [V] (p. 10).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilcoxon signed-rank with Cohen's d for RQ1/RQ2 [V] (p. 6, p. 7); Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni for paired explanation scores, Mann–Whitney for correct vs incorrect, Spearman and partial Spearman for length effects [V] (p. 5, p. 8, p. 9). No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration interaction is not significance-tested [A] (p. 8).

## 7. Key findings
1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).
2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).
3. Thinking improves P-C in 6 of 8 non-agent settings — [V] (p. 6).
4. Agent designs (means over 16 settings): SA F1 0.368 / recall 0.326 / P-C 13.7; DA F1 0.634 / recall 0.885 / precision 0.502 / P-C 6.2; MA F1 0.497 / recall 0.559 / P-C 15.8 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
5. DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR 0.882, FPR 0.880) vs SA 30.3% (FPR 0.280) and MA 55.4% (FPR 0.549); DA vs SA F1 p < 0.0001, d = 1.40; MA vs SA p = 0.0013, d = 0.92 — [V] (p. 7).
6. DA beats SA on F1 in all 16 settings and is the most stable (CV 9% vs MA 32%, SA 46%); MA has the best P-C in 11 of 16 settings, DA in none — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
7. Thinking's F1 benefit reverses with orchestration: ΔF1 +0.104 (NA), +0.100 (SA), −0.054 (DA), −0.066 (MA); ΔP-C stays positive (+1.9, +1.5, +8.1, +5.4) — [V] (p. 8, Table 5).
8. Call-matched (193 pairs, zero-shot, 2 models): 4-call self-revision has the highest mean P-C (24.7) vs SA and MA (21.9) and DA (4.7), with FPR 0.47 vs DA 0.93; the authors conclude much of the multi-agent benefit is extra inference budget — [V]/[A] (p. 11, Table 9).
9. Cost: thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking averages 25,533 tokens per sample vs 3,703 for NA; per configuration SA $27.5 / 8.0 h, DA $37.1 / 11.5 h, MA $52.7 / 14.4 h; all 64 configurations cost about $2,448, 481 kWh and 423.0M tokens — [V] (p. 10, Table 8).
10. Explanations (Nemotron-Super-49B, 59 pairs): the LLM judge rates thinking higher on completeness (+0.49), clarity (+0.51) and informativeness (+0.64); humans corroborate only informativeness (+0.30, p = 0.006) — [V] (p. 8).
11. Thinking explanations are 4.6× longer (13,579 vs 2,935 chars); controlling for length shrinks the judge's mode effect by about 40–60% but does not remove it; for Qwen3-30B no thinking advantage — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).
12. Blinded explanation quality does not differ between correct and incorrect predictions (e.g. completeness 3.58 vs 3.61, all Mann–Whitney p > 0.3); an unblinded judge creates a spurious gap (3.51 vs 2.22) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Deterministic decoding (T = 0) and a single run per configuration: results limited to deterministic decoding, no repeated-run variability (p. 11).
- [A] Prompt sensitivity and agent-design choices; configurations are representative, not task-optimal (p. 11).
- [A] Metrics may not fully capture the constructs; the rubric measures developer-facing quality, not faithfulness; a single external Claude judge may have stylistic and length preferences (p. 11).
- [A] Function-level PrimeVul Pair only; no project context, interprocedural reasoning or repository-level vulnerabilities; only four open Nemotron/Qwen models, larger models (DeepSeek-V3.1, Kimi-K2) not run due to hardware budget (p. 3, p. 11).
- [A] RQ3 manual evaluation uses a sample, which adds sampling uncertainty (p. 11).
- [A] The call-matched results are single runs and reported descriptively (p. 11).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] An "always vulnerable" classifier scores F1 = 0.667 on this balanced set (precision 0.5, recall 1.0). No reported configuration exceeds it (Table 3 max 0.665, Table 9 max 0.666), so DA's "highest F1" is near the trivial flag-everything point. Based on Table 3 (p. 7) and Table 9 (p. 11).
- [I] All P-C values are ≤26.9%, close to the 25% expected from random independent labelling of each pair member, so absolute discrimination is weak in every design. Based on Tables 2, 4 and 9 (p. 6, p. 7, p. 11).
- [I] No SAST or deep-learning baselines, so the paper says nothing about LLMs vs traditional tools. Based on Table 1 (p. 3).
- [I] Training-data contamination is not discussed; PrimeVul is public and the open models may have seen it. Based on a search of the full text for contamination or memorisation (none found).
- [I] Statistical tests on 8 or 16 paired configuration-level means have little power and no correction across RQ1/RQ2 tests; differences between individual cells should not be over-read (the authors say this too, p. 6).
- [I] Wording conflict: the abstract and conclusion say explanation gains are "largely" length-mediated (p. 11), while Section 4.3 says "substantially but not wholly" (40–60%) (p. 9).
- [I] Selection of the 193-pair subset and the handling of non-conforming outputs are not described, which limits checks on Table 9. Based on p. 5, p. 11.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): agent designs differ in number of calls and context, partly controlled by call-matched baselines (p. 7, p. 11); possible pretraining contamination not addressed; parsing rule for non-conforming outputs unspecified (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): function-level C/C++, one benchmark, four mid-size open models (p. 11).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): F1 on balanced data rewards over-flagging (authors pair it with P-C, p. 7); explanation rubric measures perceived quality, not faithfulness (p. 11).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single runs; small numbers of paired configuration means; Bonferroni applied only in RQ3 (p. 8, p. 9).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — open models, vLLM versions, hardware, prompts and replication package on Zenodo (p. 4, p. 12).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: more reasoning-oriented families (distilled DeepSeek-R1, Gemma) and larger models; costlier repository-level settings with dependency resolution, retrieval and tool support (p. 11); deeper per-model analysis and significance testing of the reasoning × orchestration interaction (p. 8).
- Suggested by us [I]: report the trivial flag-all and random baselines alongside F1/P-C; add SAST and fine-tuned DL baselines on the same pairs; repeat runs with non-zero temperature for variance.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only variants), RQ2, RQ3, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: controlled evidence that reasoning modes and multi-agent designs mainly shift the recall/false-positive trade-off rather than improving discrimination, with detailed energy, token and USD costs. Useful for RQ3 (cost vs benefit of agentic LLM designs) and RQ2 (F1 vs pairwise metrics), and consistent with yildiz2025benchmarking's finding that F1 hides near-random pairwise accuracy. No traditional or DL baseline, so it does not inform LLM-vs-SAST directly.

# SecVulEval: Context-Aware Benchmarking of LLMs for Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Ahmed, Md Basim Uddin; Harzevili, Nima Shiri; Shin, Jiho; Pham, Hung Viet; Wang, Song
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 3rd ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3805760.3814932 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3805760.3814932
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

> Version note: the text analysed is the arXiv preprint 2505.19828v1 (26 May 2025), titled "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1). The published AIware 2026 version may differ in title, numbers and content. See Analyst notes.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Build a C/C++ vulnerability benchmark with statement-level labels, rich metadata and program context (function arguments, external functions, type declarations, globals, execution environment), and use it to test how well current LLMs detect and localise real vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] Motivation: existing datasets (BigVul, CVEFixes, DiverseVul, PrimeVul, MegaVul, etc.) are function-level only, lack context, contain duplicates/mislabels, and line-level labels (BigVul, CVEFixes, SVEN) are line fragments rather than statements (p. 2, p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs or hypotheses. Two experiments: (1) LLM vulnerability detection at function and statement level; (2) LLM identification of the context needed for detection (p. 6, p. 7).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: benchmark construction from NVD + GitHub commits, followed by an empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs inside a multi-agent pipeline, with manual judging of statement-level outputs (p. 4-p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention: five-agent pipeline: Normalization Agent (tree-sitter AST, no LLM), Planning Agent (function summary + checklist of up to 8 red-flag cues), Context Agent (asks for up to 6 external symbols per round, max 3 rounds; definitions fetched with tree-sitter), Detection Agent (verdict + vulnerable statements + reason), Validation Agent (agrees or disagrees; Detection reruns up to 3 times) (p. 7, p. 14-p. 16). [A] Authors claim it is the first LLM multi-agent pipeline applied to vulnerability detection (p. 7).
- Models: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, Deepseek-Coder-33B-Instruct, Codestral-22B-v0.1 (open weights, HuggingFace), GPT-4.1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (p. 8).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: only the 5 LLMs are compared. No static-analysis tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM detector, no single-LLM (non-agent) baseline, and no with/without-context ablation for detection (not reported).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): NVD CVEs (non-REJECTED) for products previously identified as C/C++ in BigVul, CVEFixes and PrimeVul, plus NVD keyword search ("C++", "C language", ".cpp"); only CVEs with an NVD "Patch" reference to a commit in the original (non-forked) repository; commit data via GitHub REST API (p. 4).
- Sampling / selection method: non-C/C++ files removed; only single-commit fixes kept (43 multi-commit CVEs dropped); files with no function changes removed; tangled changes filtered by keeping only functions solely modified in a file or named in the CVE/commit message; de-duplication by md5 of whitespace-normalised function text (p. 5). Detection experiment: 300 functions randomly selected from the Top-25 CWE types, manually validated; 120 of them vulnerable (p. 8, p. 12, p. 13).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 25,440 functions = 10,998 vulnerable + 14,442 non-vulnerable; 5,867 CVEs, 707 projects, 145 CWEs, CVEs from 1999-2024 (p. 6, p. 9). Function size 4-541 lines (2.5-97.5 percentile), median 44 lines; on average about 4 statements deleted and 6 added per function (p. 6). Linux alone contributes 1,920 CVEs and 2,793 vulnerable functions (p. 5).
- Non-vulnerable functions: the exact definition (fixed versions of vulnerable functions vs. other unchanged functions) is not stated explicitly. The text says both "vulnerable version" and "fixed version" copies are kept for each changed function (p. 5).
- Context labels: generated automatically by GPT-4.1 from CWE, function body, patch, commit message and CVE description. A manual check of 100 random samples (4 excluded as N/A) gave 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy (99% CI) (p. 6).
- Data availability: dataset on HuggingFace (arag0rn/SecVulEval) and code on GitHub (basimbd/SecVulEval) (p. 3); "friendly license" for research and commercial use (p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: pass@1, temperature 0.1; Intel Xeon Gold 6442Y CPU, 4 x NVIDIA L40S GPUs, 250 GiB RAM; open models via transformers.pipeline (p. 8, p. 17). Prompts for all four LLM agents are given verbatim. They were rewritten to stress *defensive* research after models refused to answer (p. 13-p. 16). Function and AST inputs "could be truncated if too long" (p. 14); the truncation limit is not reported.
- Statement-level TP rules (manual): exact vulnerable statements with correct reasoning; or at least one of several fix locations; or correct statements plus at most two unrelated ones; or only the sink statement / sink + source with correct reasoning (p. 8). Function level is judged automatically from the `is_vulnerable` field (p. 8).
- Number and independence of manual raters, and inter-rater agreement: not reported.
- Cost/time: open models take 4.97-7.99 minutes per function in total (Codestral 4.97, Qwen 6.03, Deepseek 7.99) (p. 17). Time for the proprietary models and API cost are not reported (p. 17).
- Code availability: GitHub repository (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: precision, recall and F1 at function level (is the function vulnerable?) and statement level (are the vulnerable statements identified with correct reasoning?). A function-level TP with wrong reasoning is defined as a statement-level FN (p. 7). Context identification: accuracy per context type versus dataset ground truth, which is itself GPT-4.1-generated (p. 6, p. 7, p. 9).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests compare the function length of detected vs. missed vulnerable functions (p. 12, p. 13). The detection metrics have no confidence intervals or significance tests, and repeated runs are not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Statement-level detection is poor for all models: F1 = Claude-3.7-Sonnet 23.83%, GPT-4.1 22.38%, Codestral-22B 15.31%, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 13.57%, Deepseek-Coder-33B 7.14% — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
2. Function-level F1: Claude 53.89%, GPT-4.1 52.25%, Codestral 46.61%, Deepseek 45.71%, Qwen 35.20%. Function-level precision is only 35.48-47.41% for every model — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
3. The proprietary models are more "aggressive": function-level recall is 75.63% (Claude) and 73.11% (GPT-4.1), but precision is 41.86% and 40.65%, lower than Codestral (47.41%) and Deepseek (45.16%). Of 300 samples (120 vulnerable), GPT-4.1 and Claude flagged 214 and 215 as vulnerable vs. 116-124 for the open models — [V] (p. 8, p. 13).
4. Statement-level precision is 5.65-15.35% for all models, i.e. most flagged statements/reasons are wrong — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
5. Detected vulnerable functions are much shorter than missed ones: median 14-33 LoC detected vs. 64-71 LoC missed; one-sided Mann-Whitney U p = 0.000197-0.0168 for all five models — [V] (p. 12, p. 13, Table 5).
6. Over-detection concentrates on CWE-476 (NULL dereference, flagged even when an explicit null check exists), CWE-416 (any `free()`/`kfree()` treated as use-after-free) and CWE-190 (arithmetic flagged as overflow without analysis), especially for GPT-4.1 and Claude. This is qualitative, from manual validation; no counts are given — [A] (p. 13).
7. LLMs identify the needed context poorly. The best per type is Claude (external functions 37.00%, type definitions 41.33%, globals 34.53%). Function-argument accuracy is 0-5.31% for all models, and no model identified any environment-level context (1.5% of all contexts) — [V] (p. 9, Table 4).
8. GPT-4.1 identifies the required context with 82.98 ± 9.68% accuracy when given the patch, CVE and commit message. This is the dataset-construction setting, not detection — [V] (p. 6).
9. SecVulEval has 0.0% duplicates vs. 18.9% (CVEFixes), 12.7% (BigVul) and 3.3% (DiverseVul) as reported by PrimeVul. The SecVulEval figure is the authors' own; the others are cited from their ref. [5] — [V] (p. 3, Table 1).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Context labels were produced by an LLM; manual validation covered only 100 samples; "relevant context" is subjective; repository-wide / transitive context is not covered (p. 12).
- [A] Manual statement-level judging is subjective and labour-intensive, which limits scale (p. 12).
- [A] Only the largest runnable size of each model was evaluated; conclusions may not hold for smaller sizes (p. 12).
- [A] Multi-commit fixes were excluded for simplicity (p. 5).
- [A] The dataset could be misused to train models to exploit vulnerabilities (p. 12).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] There is no non-LLM baseline at all (no SAST tool, no fine-tuned DL/PLM model, no single-prompt LLM). So the paper cannot say whether the multi-agent design helps or hurts, or how LLMs compare with traditional tools. Based on §3/§5 above.
- [I] The statement-level recall in Table 3 appears not to follow the stated definition. We reconstructed integer counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (e.g. Claude: 215 flagged, 90 function-level TP, 119 positives, 33 statement-level TP). Every reported statement-level recall is reproduced exactly as TP_stat / (TP_stat + function-level FN). That means "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as FN, contrary to the definition on p. 7. Under the stated definition, Claude's statement-level recall would be about 27.7% (33/119), not 53.23%, and its F1 about 19.8%, not 23.83%. The same pattern holds for all five models (GPT-4.1: about 26.1% vs. 49.21%). This is our arithmetic on the paper's tables (p. 8, p. 13). It makes the headline numbers optimistic, not pessimistic.
- [I] The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119-126), although the paper says 120 of 300 are vulnerable (p. 13). This suggests unreported per-model exclusions (e.g. failed outputs). Same reconstruction as above.
- [I] The detection evaluation uses only 300 functions (about 1.2% of the benchmark), drawn from Top-25 CWEs only, with no uncertainty reported. Gaps of a few points between models (e.g. Claude vs. GPT-4.1, 23.83% vs. 22.38%) are probably within sampling noise. Based on p. 8.
- [I] Experiment 2 is circular: the context "ground truth" was generated by GPT-4.1 (p. 6), and GPT-4.1 is also one of the evaluated models (p. 9). This makes the context accuracies hard to interpret.
- [I] The task differs from SAST use. The pipeline gets one function plus LLM-requested definitions, not the whole repository or build. The results describe LLM review of single functions, not project-scale scanning.
- [I] The 300-sample set is 40% vulnerable, far more than in real codebases, so precision would likely drop further in deployment. This rests on the 120/300 count (p. 13).
- [I] Data contamination is not discussed: CVEs up to 2024 and their public fixes may be in the training data of all five models, and there is no time-split analysis.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): the manual judging rules are lenient (sink-only counts as TP; up to two extra statements allowed) (p. 8). The number of raters and their agreement are not reported. There is also the recall inconsistency in §9. Heuristics reduce label noise, but noise in the vulnerability labels is never measured; only the context labels were validated (p. 5, p. 6). De-duplication removes exact duplicates only (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ only. Linux is a large share (2,793 of 10,998 vulnerable functions) (p. 5). The evaluation covers only Top-25 CWEs and 300 samples (p. 8), and five specific LLM versions at temperature 0.1 (p. 8).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): "correct reasoning" is a human judgement with no stated protocol beyond the four rules (p. 8). Function-level detection is judged without checking whether the stated reason is right (p. 7, p. 8).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): only one run per model is reported, with no confidence intervals or tests on Table 3. The Mann-Whitney tests run across five models without multiple-comparison correction, but all p < 0.017, so they are likely robust (p. 13).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): the dataset, code and full prompts are released (p. 3, p. 14-p. 16), and hardware and temperature are reported (p. 8, p. 17). Whether the manual judgements for the 300 samples are released is not stated.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: use the statement-level and context labels to train and evaluate detection models (p. 10); test smaller model sizes (p. 12); "advancing statement-level detection is essential" (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools (e.g. CodeQL, Cppcheck) and fine-tuned DL detectors on the same 300-sample subset; report statement-level recall under the stated definition with confidence intervals; compare the multi-agent pipeline against a single prompt, with and without context; split by CVE date to check for contamination.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (benchmark quality, granularity, duplication), RQ4 (C/C++, CWE-specific over-detection, function length), RQ5 (context, localisation, false positives). Indirectly RQ3 (agentic LLM pipeline with AST/tree-sitter context; execution time) and RQ1 (absolute effectiveness of LLMs alone, no head-to-head comparison).
- How it informs our work [I]: strong evidence that function-level LLM scores overstate real capability. When the correct root cause is required, F1 drops by more than half. Useful for the "evaluation realism" argument and for CWE-level weaknesses (false alarms on CWE-476/416/190). It cannot answer RQ1 directly because there is no SAST or DL comparison.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Best LLM (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, multi-agent) reaches 23.83% statement-level F1 and 53.89% function-level F1 on real C/C++ CVEs; function-level precision ≤47.41% for all 5 LLMs; no SAST/DL baseline | p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Requiring correct vulnerable statements + reasoning cuts F1 by more than half vs. function-level labels (e.g. GPT-4.1 52.25% → 22.38%) | p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | SecVulEval: 25,440 de-duplicated C/C++ functions, 5,867 CVEs, 145 CWEs, statement-level + context labels; prior datasets have up to 18.9% duplicates | p. 3, p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Statement-level recall appears computed without counting wrong-reasoning cases as FN; under the stated definition Claude's recall would be ~27.7% (not 53.23%) and F1 ~19.8% | p. 7, p. 8, p. 13 | I | moderate |

| RQ3 | Multi-agent pipeline with open 22-33B models costs ~5-8 min per function on 4 x L40S | p. 17 | V | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "The best-performing Claude-3.7-Sonnet model achieves 23.83% F1-score for detecting vulnerable statements with correct reasoning, with GPT-4.1 closely behind." (p. 1)

> "If the model correctly identifies a function as vulnerable, but the reasoning is incorrect, we consider this a True Positive for function-level detection but a False Negative for statement-level detection" (p. 7)

> "every model is significantly more successful at recognizing vulnerabilities in compact, shorter functions and consistently misses them in the longer ones." (p. 13)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: the whole preprint was read (pp. 1-17), including appendices A-E (limitations, failure analysis, prompts, execution time). References were skimmed.
- Version / identity: `metadata.json` describes the AIware 2026 proceedings paper "SecVulEval: Context-Aware Benchmarking of LLMs for Vulnerability Detection" (DOI 10.1145/3805760.3814932). The PDF is arXiv 2505.19828v1, titled "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", with the same five authors (Ahmed, Shiri Harzevili, Shin, Pham, Wang; York University); confirmed on PDF p. 1. rlab flagged identity UNCONFIRMED only because the title changed. This analysis is based on the preprint, so numbers in the published version may differ. If the published version becomes accessible, re-check Table 3 and the recall definition.
- Uncertainties: (1) The Table 3 reconstruction (§9) uses the smallest integer counts consistent with all reported percentages and with the flag counts on p. 13 (for Codestral, GPT-4.1 and Claude). It reproduces all 30 percentages, but it is our inference, not something the authors state. (2) The definition of non-vulnerable functions (fixed versions vs. unrelated functions) is not explicit. (3) The appendix calls Qwen "Qwen2.5-Coder-33B" (p. 13), while elsewhere it is 32B (p. 8); this looks like a typo. (4) Our reconstruction implies Qwen flagged 124 functions and Deepseek 124, while p. 13 says 121 and 124.
- Tier: published (AIware 2026, peer-reviewed conference), but the analysed text is the preprint, which was not peer-reviewed.

4.3       Evaluation Metrics

In this work, we use Precision, Recall, and F1-Score to measure the vulnerability detection perfor-
mance of the models. Specifically, vulnerable instances are regarded as positive, and non-vulnerable
instances as negative. For statement-level vulnerability detection, we measure a prediction as True
Positive if it correctly predicts vulnerable statements along with accurate reasoning. If the model
correctly identifies a function as vulnerable, but the reasoning is incorrect, we consider this a True
Positive for function-level detection but a False Negative for statement-level detection since it misses
the correct vulnerability. Precision measures the likelihood that a prediction is correct when it
identifies an instance as positive. Recall, on the other hand, measures the ability to correctly identify
all the positive instances, even if the model makes some False Positives. Finally, F1-Score is the
harmonic mean of both Precision and Recall.

C     Failure Analysis of LLMs on Vulnerability Detection
C.1   Effects of Function Size

To determine whether the function length has distinctive effects on the performance of the LLMs,
we performed a thorough analysis. We partitioned the complete set of 120 true-positive functions
(from our subset of 300 samples) into those correctly flagged by each model and those it failed to
detect. Then, we compared the two groups’ lines-of-code (LoC) distributions. For each model, we
applied a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test to each model independently, assessing the hypothesis that
  function returned immediately, precluding any later use of tmp_path. Finally, many arithmetic
  operations were flagged as Integer Overflow (CWE-190) without sufficient analysis to determine if
  an overflow or wraparound condition could occur.
  These tendencies for over-detection were particularly pronounced in GPT-4.1 and Claude-3.7-Sonnet,
  which exhibited a more aggressive vulnerability flagging behavior. From the set of 300 samples,
  comprising 120 genuinely vulnerable functions, GPT-4.1 and Claude-3.7-Sonnet identified 214 and
  215 functions as vulnerable, respectively. In contrast, Qwen2.5-Coder-33B, Deepseek-Coder-33B,
  and Codestral-22B demonstrated a more conservative approach, flagging only 121, 124, and 116
  functions as vulnerable, which resulted in a significantly lower incidence of false positives.
